# Playbook

**When I'm told the sustainable share, I start there.** It's the rate that keeps the stock flat. In any season except the last, catching the sustainable share guarantees I earn the same amount every remaining season. Deviating upward costs me more in lost future seasons than it gains in the current one, because the stock drop compounds.

**In the final season, I go aggressive.** There is no next season to protect. I submit a large share of the remaining stock — at minimum the stock divided by the number of boats, and possibly more if I believe the others will be conservative. The entire game's payoff is front-loaded into this one number, so being timid here is the single biggest way to leave points on the table.

**I do not overfish in early seasons to "get ahead."** A small overage in season 1 shrank my per-season income for every subsequent season. The compounding loss outweighs the one-time gain. If I want to extract extra value, the final season is where I do it, not scattered across the middle.

**I watch what the other boats actually catch, not what I expect them to catch.** If they are consistently overfishing, the stock will drop regardless of my restraint. In that case I adjust my expectation of the stock trajectory rather than assuming it stays flat, and I lean slightly harder into the final-season grab because the middle seasons will be worth less.

**If the stock is dropping season over season, I do not try to compensate by cutting my own catch below sustainable.** The others' overfishing is already driving the decline; my extra restraint doesn't stop it, it just gives them more. I hold at sustainable (or slightly above if the stock is still healthy) and save my aggression for the last round.

**If the stock is stable and everyone is at sustainable, I stay put through the middle seasons and concentrate all my extra ambition into the final round.** This is the cleanest way to maximize total: reliable income for N−1 seasons plus one big final grab.

**I do not try to outsmart the others into a "tragedy of the commons" standoff in the middle seasons.** If I'm the only one restricting while others overfish, I'm the one losing. The only rational deviation from sustainable is upward, and the only rational time for that is the last season.

**Playbook: Ref Commons (Fishery)**

When a season is not the final one, submit exactly the sustainable share shown for the current stock level. Do not overfish to freeride — the one-time gain is smaller than the compounding loss in future sustainable yield.

When the final season is put to me, take the entire remaining stock (or as much as is available). There is no future season to preserve, so the only constraint is what the harbour will record as landable. Do not leave fish in the water.

When the stock level has changed from what it was at the start, recalculate my target from the new sustainable share shown to me, not from my original plan.

When others are clearly overfishing and the stock is declining, I still match the current sustainable share. I do not overfish in retaliation or to "get ahead" of a collapse I cannot prevent unilaterally — if the stock collapses, I get zero either way.

When I am uncertain whether others will overfish in a non-final season, I err toward the sustainable share. A modest overfishing gamble only pays off if the stock survives, and the downside (reduced yield every remaining season) is nearly always larger than the upside.

2.text:
# Playbook

When the game is the last season, take as much as the stock allows. There is no future to protect, so the sustainable share is irrelevant. Submit the full stock or close to it.

When the game is not the last season, first check what the other boats did last season. If they are each taking roughly the sustainable share, I can take a small premium (about 10–20% above the sustainable share) because my extra catch only reduces the stock by half next season and the others will absorb the difference without changing their behaviour.

When the game is not the last season and the stock has dropped below its starting value, do not try to "save" it by taking less than the sustainable share. Taking less than the sustainable share while others take the full share only slows the decline without helping me; it is strictly worse than taking the sustainable share.

When I notice another boat taking significantly more than the sustainable share for two or more consecutive seasons, match their take. If the stock is declining because of a free rider, I should not be the one left behind taking a smaller share of a shrinking pie.

When the stock is at or near the cap (100), I can afford to take a larger premium in the current season because the regrowth is already maximised and the stock will snap back to the cap next season regardless.

When in doubt between two options in a non-final season, choose the one that is slightly higher. The cost of overfishing by a small amount is spread across future seasons and is usually less than the immediate gain, especially with fewer than four seasons remaining.

Do not anchor on the "sustainable share" number as a moral limit. It is the cooperative equilibrium, not the individual optimum. My score depends only on my total, not on the stock's health per se. The stock matters only insofar as it determines what I can take in future seasons.
